questions.prompt: Why do two .pf files exist for the same executable name?
options: Windows creates a backup copy of every prefetch file
The hash suffix is derived from the executable's full path, so the same filename run from two different directories produces two separate files
One file holds timestamps and the other holds the referenced-file list
The second file is created after eight executions
questions.explanation: Because the hash encodes the full path, two .pf files for the same name mean the binary ran from two distinct locations -- and only one of those is likely legitimate.

questions.prompt: Why is an empty C:\Windows\Prefetch directory on a server not evidence of anti-forensics?
options: Servers store prefetch data in the registry instead
Prefetch is disabled by default on Windows Server, so absence is expected -- EnablePrefetcher must be checked before interpreting it
Prefetch files are automatically deleted after 24 hours on servers
Servers never execute programs that would generate prefetch
questions.explanation: Treating a missing .pf as proof a program never ran produces a wrong conclusion on every server. The EnablePrefetcher value determines whether absence means anything at all.

questions.prompt: What makes the referenced-file list inside a .pf particularly valuable?
options: It lists every file the program has ever opened
It records files and directories referenced during the first ten seconds of execution, which can reveal what a since-deleted binary touched
It contains the program's source code
It stores the SHA-1 hash of each referenced file
questions.explanation: When the binary itself is gone, that list of DLLs and paths is often the only surviving record of what it interacted with.

questions.prompt: How many execution timestamps does a modern .pf file retain?
options: Unlimited, until the file is deleted
questions.explanation: Windows 8 and later store the last eight execution times; Windows 7 and earlier kept only the most recent one.
